'''Jane Smiley Cronin Scanlon''' (July 17, 1922 – June 19, 2018) was an American mathematician and an [[emeritus professor]] of mathematics at [[Rutgers University]]. Her research concerned [[partial differential equation]]s and [[mathematical biology]].<ref name="awm">{{citation|url=http://www.math.unl.edu/~awm/awm_folder/NoetherBrochure/Scanlon85.html|title=Jane Cronin Scanlon|work=Profiles of Women in Mathematics|publisher=[[Association for Women in Mathematics]]|access-date=2018-11-01|archive-date=2008-09-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080907163544/http://www.math.unl.edu/~awm/awm_folder/NoetherBrochure/Scanlon85.html|url-status=dead}}.</ref><ref name="riddle">{{citation|url=http://www.agnesscott.edu/lriddle/women/scanlon.htm|title=Jane Cronin Scanlon|first=Larry|last=Riddle|work=Biographies of Women Mathematicians|publisher=[[Agnes Scott College]]|access-date=2014-12-25}}.</ref>

==Education and career==
Scanlon earned a bachelor's degree in mathematics from Wayne University (now [[Wayne State University]]).<ref name=obit/> She completed her Ph.D. in mathematics at the [[University of Michigan]] in 1949, under the supervision of [[Erich Rothe]]. Her dissertation was ''Branch Points of Solutions of Equations in Banach Space''.<ref name="awm"/><ref name="riddle"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=Jane Smiley Cronin Scanlon|id=5743}}</ref>

After working for the [[United States Air Force]] and the American Optical Company, she returned to academia as a lecturer at [[Wheaton College (Massachusetts)]] and then [[Stonehill College]].
She moved to the [[Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn]] in 1957, and to Rutgers in 1965. In 1974 Scanlon was elected as an [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]] Member at Large and held the position until 1976.<ref>{{Cite web |title=AMS Committees |url=http://www.ams.org/about-us/governance/committees/mal-past.html |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=American Mathematical Society |language=en}}</ref> She retired in 1991.<ref name="awm"/><ref name="riddle"/><ref>{{citation|title=Women Succeeding in the Sciences: Theories and Practices Across Disciplines|first=Jody|last=Bart|publisher=Purdue University Press|year=2000|isbn=9781557531216|page=92|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=baK6XSXhrS8C&pg=PA92}}.</ref> During her twenty-six years at Rutgers, she supervised seven doctoral students.<ref name=obitAMS>{{cite journal|author=Aboufadel, Edward F.|title=In Memoriam: Jane Smiley Cronin Scanlon|journal=Notices of the AMS|date=October 2019|volume=66|issue=9|pages=1448–1452|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/201909/rnoti-p1448.pdf|doi=10.1090/noti1948|doi-access=free}}</ref>

She died in June 2018 at the age of 95.<ref name=obit>[https://www.krowickigorny.com/notices/DrJaneCronin-Scanlon Obituary for Dr. Jane Cronin Scanlon]</ref>

==Recognition==
Scanlon was a [[Noether Lecture]]r in 1985,<ref name="awm"/> and [[Pi Mu Epsilon]] J. Sutherland Frame Lecturer in 1989.<ref name=pme>[https://pme-math.org/j-sutherland-frame-lectures-2 J. Sutherland Frame Lectures], [[Pi Mu Epsilon]]</ref> Her talks concerned "[[Entrainment (physics)|entrainment of frequency]]" and the application of this principle to mathematical models of the [[Purkinje fibers]] in the [[heart]].<ref name="awm"/><ref name=pme/> In 2012, she became one of the inaugural [[fellow]]s of the [[American Mathematical Society]].<ref>[http://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society], retrieved 2014-12-25.</ref>

==Personal life==
She married the physicist Joseph Scanlon in 1953. The two divorced in 1979.<ref name=obitAMS/> Upon her death, she was survived by four children and seven grandchildren.<ref name=obit/>
